lessons.title: Listening: Pick from a List (Section 2-3)
lessons.grammar_topic: Pick from a list (listening) — ro'yxatdan ikki (yoki uch) javob tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz bergan audiolar (Track 23 Irina survey, Track 11 Joe devices) va 3 ta mualliflik skripti.
objectives: "Choose TWO letters" listening savolida ikkala javobni ham eshitib topish.
Savol va 5 ta variantni (A–E) tinglashdan OLDIN o'qib, kalit so'zlarni belgilash.
Chalg'ituvchi variantlarni ajratish: audioda tilga olinadi, lekin inkor qilinadi yoki boshqa narsa haqida.
Har javob alohida ball olishini bilish — bittasini eshitib qolsangiz ham yozing.
5 ta mashqda (2 ta ustoz audiosi + 3 ta skript) ishlash.
timeline: Salomlashish, o'tgan darsdagi savol turini 3 savolda eslatish
Ustoz doskada: qoida, bosqichlar, tipik xatolar
Savol turiga oid mashq birga bajariladi, har javob izohlanadi
Matndagi va savoldagi so'zlar jadvali; o'quvchilar ovoz chiqarib topadi
Mustaqil bajariladi, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi
Skript ustoz tomonidan o'qiladi yoki audio qo'yiladi, keyin transkript bilan tekshiriladi
Xatolar daftari: har xato javob sababi bilan yoziladi

intro: Listening pick from a list — savol va 5 ta variant (A–E) beriladi, ulardan IKKITASI to'g'ri. Ba'zan Section 3 da uchtasi.
Ikkala harf ham alohida ball: 7–8-savol = 2 ball. Tartib muhim emas: "B, C" = "C, B".
Eng muhim qoida: variantlarni tinglashdan OLDIN o'qing. Audioda vaqt kam — kalit so'zlarni oldindan bilsangiz, tez ilg'aysiz.
Barcha 5 variant audioda biror shaklda tilga olinadi. "Eshitildi" degani "javob" degani emas — variant TASDIQLANDIMI yoki INKOR qilindimi, shuni tinglang.
Chalg'ituvchining ikki turi: 1) variant aytiladi, keyin rad etiladi ("I was thinking of buying a calculator, but I decided it wasn't necessary"); 2) variant boshqa kishi/narsa haqida.
Section 2 — monolog (bitta so'zlovchi); Section 3 — suhbat (2–4 kishi). Kim gapirayotganini kuzating.
presentation: Yozing — har javob alohida ball. Ikkinchisiga eng ehtimollisini tanlang.
Yo'q. "A, C" va "C, A" bir xil.
Tasdiqlangan ikkitasini oling; qolganlari rad etilgan yoki boshqa narsa haqida.
Keyingi savol boshlanishidan oldingi pauzada o'qing; audio to'xtamaydi.
Uchinchisini qayta o'ylang: u aniq tasdiqlandimi yoki faqat tilga olindimi?
notes: Track 23 (Irina) va Track 11 (Joe) — 12-darsdagi Irina va Joe suhbatlarining davomi. Bir mavzu ikki savol turi bilan.
Ustoz kaliti yuborilmagan — javoblar transkriptdan Jony Academy tomonidan yechildi. Kitob kaliti bo'lsa, solishtirib tekshiring.
Har javobdan keyin so'rang: "qaysi so'z tasdiqladi? qaysi variant nega rad etildi?"
Chalg'ituvchi tahlili — darsning asosiy ishi: har rad etilgan variant audioda qanday eshitilgani yozdiriladi.

class_ex.title: Tasdiq yoki inkor?
class_ex.instr: Ustoz gap o'qiydi; o'quvchi "javob (tasdiq)" yoki "chalg'ituvchi (inkor)" deydi.
items: "I was thinking of buying a calculator, but I decided it wasn't necessary."
"The audio quality was crisp and clear — ten out of ten."
"The choice of radio stations seemed very limited."
"I always feel I'm going to get stuck in one." (revolving doors)
why: "but ... wasn't necessary".
Sotib olgan.
Radio ovozi yaxshi.
Kam stansiya.
"not so keen on".
class_ex.note: Signal so'zlar doskada: but, however, not, decided not, I'm not keen on (inkor); really like, that's great, definitely (tasdiq).

listenings.title: Track 23. Irina at the electronics exhibition — a survey
intro: So'rovnoma o'tkazuvchi ayol Irina bilan gaplashmoqda (12-darsdagi Track 22 dan keyin). Avval 7–10-savollar va A–E variantlarni o'qing, kalit so'zlarni belgilang. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose TWO letters, A–E for each question. Har savolda IKKI javob.
transcript: WOMAN: Excuse me.
IRINA: Yes?
WOMAN: Before you go through, I wonder if you could help us by answering a few questions for a survey. It won't take long.
IRINA: No problem. We're not in any hurry.
WOMAN: Fine, thanks. Now, er, let's look at the questions. First one. Why are you visiting the exhibition?

IRINA: Well, I want to keep up with the latest developments in electronics, you know – I was recommended by a friend to come here and see what new devices and inventions are coming out and learn a bit. I mean, I don't generally go shopping for new electronics – I'm not the sort of person who goes out and buys all the latest gadgets – the prices are too high when they're new. But it interests me, and I thought also there would be things which would interest my son and he'd enjoy it as well, so that's why we're here.
WOMAN: OK ... and here's a question to find out what sort of consumer you are. Have you bought any electronics recently?

IRINA: Recently? Sure. I was thinking of buying a new calculator for the office, but I decided it wasn't really necessary because I can do all the calculations just as easily on a computer. Anyway, I got a new laptop recently, you know, they have so many applications and they don't take up much space either. Better to have lots of things on the same device, I think. The other thing I bought was a present for my husband's birthday. I thought it would be nice to have a record of our holidays, so I bought him a camera, and I'm hoping to get him more interested in photography.
WOMAN: Right ... and here's a question about this building. I know you haven't had a chance to look around a lot yet, but at first sight, what do you think of it?

IRINA: Oh, it looks pretty good to me. It's got lots of natural light, so you don't have to put up with lots of electric lighting, which is quite tiring on the eyes. It feels very large and spacious, which is great because although it's full of activity and quite noisy, it doesn't feel too crowded. Also, when you look up at the ceiling near the entrance, with the design of stars and planets on it, that's something I really like. I'm not so keen on those revolving doors, though. I always feel I'm going to get stuck in one.
WOMAN: Did you have any difficulties getting to the exhibition?

IRINA: Well, coming at this time of day the roads weren't too busy, so that was all right, and there were plenty of signposts, so the car park was easy to find. The only problem was it was full when I arrived – I guess I should have come earlier – so I had to find another one quite a long walk away, which was a pity. Then we had to stand outside for quite a long time queuing to get in – this exhibition is pretty popular. That was a bit of a problem, because my son gets impatient, but fortunately it wasn't raining, otherwise we might have gone home.

tasks.title: Questions 7–10: Choose TWO letters, A–E
tasks.instr: Har savolda ikki javob. Har variant uchun tasdiq/inkorni belgilang.
items: 7 Which TWO reasons does Irina give for visiting the exhibition? A) to meet a friend B) to improve her knowledge C) to buy something D) to check prices E) to entertain her child
8 Which TWO devices has Irina bought recently? A) a calculator B) a computer C) a camera D) a phone E) a digital recorder
9 What TWO things does Irina like about the building? A) the electric lights B) the space C) the activity D) the ceiling E) the entrance
10 Which TWO problems did Irina have coming to the exhibition? A) driving in heavy traffic B) finding the car park C) parking the car D) waiting to enter E) standing outside in the rain
why: "Keep up with the latest developments ... learn a bit" (B) va "things which would interest my son and he'd enjoy it" (E). A tuzoq: do'st TAVSIYA qilgan, uchrashish uchun emas. C teskari: "I don't generally go shopping". D — narx yuqori, lekin tekshirish maqsad emas.
"I got a new laptop recently" (B — computer) va "I bought him a camera" (C). A tuzoq: kalkulyator — "decided it wasn't really necessary", sotib olmagan.

"It feels very large and spacious" (B) va "the ceiling near the entrance ... that's something I really like" (D). A tuzoq: tabiiy yorug'lik yoqadi, elektr yorug'lik "tiring on the eyes". E tuzoq: shift kirish yonida, lekin u SHIFTni yaxshi ko'radi.
To'xtash joyi to'lgan, boshqa joy topgan (C) va "stand outside ... queuing to get in" (D). A teskari: "roads weren't too busy". B teskari: "car park was easy to find". E teskari: "it wasn't raining".
tasks.note: Jony Academy javoblari (transkript bo'yicha): 7 B,E · 8 B,C · 9 B,D · 10 C,D. Kitob kaliti bo'lsa solishtiring.

tasks.title: Chalg'ituvchi tahlili
tasks.instr: Har rad etilgan variant audioda qanday eshitildi?
answers: "you don't have to put up with lots of electric lighting"
"the car park was easy to find"
why: Sotib olmagan.
Tabiiy yorug'lik yaxshi.
Muammo — to'lgani.
Yomg'ir yo'q edi.

listenings.title: Track 11. Joe tests three devices
listenings.qtype: Pick from a list (1–4) — qo'shimcha mashq
intro: Joe uchta qurilmani sinab ko'rgan: mobil telefon, radio va noutbuk. Avval savollarni va variantlarni o'qing. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Choose TWO letters, A–E for each question.
transcript: WOMAN: Right, Joe. Let's move on. Now, we gave you three items to test for us. Let's start with the mobile phone.
JOE: OK. Well, it has its good points and its bad points. The purple and silver make it quite eye-catching, you know, modern, exciting.
WOMAN: Right. Anything else?
JOE: Well, it's very small, isn't it? I know people say small is good, but in this case, I think you might have gone too far.
WOMAN: In what way?

JOE: It can be a bit difficult to use, especially if you've got big hands like mine. You press one key and you end up pressing another at the same time. On the other hand, thanks to the oval design, it does fit comfortably in your hand. Mobiles are usually sort of rectangular, aren't they? I think this is much better.
WOMAN: OK. What else?

JOE: When I was sending text messages, I had real problems seeing what I was writing. It's not that the screen was too small, just that it was a bit dark. If you're outside, you can hardly see anything on it.
WOMAN: We added a few things that you don't get on other mobiles. What did you think about those?
JOE: Ah, right. Well, that noise it makes if you move away from it? That's really annoying. It's basically a good idea, but I think that after a while, it would drive me mad.
WOMAN: So you probably wouldn't buy it?

JOE: Probably not. When I buy a mobile phone, I don't want one that's going to be difficult to operate. There's no point having a phone that looks good if you have to spend ages trying to make a call or send a text message. It's funny, but I find that more expensive mobile phones are more difficult to use than cheaper ones. It should be the other way round. So keep it simple. And I want a phone that doesn't have problems picking up a signal or doesn't cut you off halfway through a call. And all those games and other things you get on a mobile, I really can't see the point in those.
WOMAN: Fair point. Next, the digital radio. What did you think?
JOE: The audio quality was crisp and clear. Even if you turned it up really loud, some sound systems can sound a bit distorted at higher volumes, but not on this one. So ten out of ten for that.
WOMAN: Great.

JOE: The thing is, I'm not sure if it's the area I live in, but the choice of radio stations seemed very limited. It didn't make any difference what I did with the aerial or where I put the radio, high up on a shelf, low down on the floor. And there seemed to be a delay when you turned up the volume.
WOMAN: What do you mean?
JOE: Well, when you press the volume control, for example, nothing seems to happen for a few seconds. And the same thing happens when you want to change radio stations.
WOMAN: Hmm, OK. The third item was the laptop computer. What's your opinion on that?

JOE: Oh, I really liked it. It's so small, so compact, but easy to use at the same time. I don't think you could make it smaller if you tried. But at 900 pounds, I'm not sure you'd get many customers. That's a lot of money for a laptop. Bring that down to, say, 400 pounds and things might be different.
WOMAN: Any other changes you'd make, like adding more memory, for example?

JOE: Oh, I think that's fine as it is. 300 gigabytes of memory is probably more than enough for most people. Oh, and incidentally, the way the keyboard folds out so that it's like a full-sized one, that's really clever. But the computer doesn't have anywhere you can play CD-ROMs. And I'd include a light in the keyboard so you can use it when it's dark.

tasks.title: Questions 1–4: Choose TWO letters, A–E
items: 1 What TWO things did Joe like about the mobile phone? A) its colour B) its size C) its shape D) its screen E) its unique features

2 What TWO things does Joe usually look for when he buys a mobile phone? A) It should be easy to use. B) It should look good. C) It should be cheap. D) It should be reliable. E) It should have a variety of games.

3 Which TWO problems did Joe have with the radio? A) It didn't sound good. B) It wasn't loud enough. C) It didn't pick up many radio stations. D) He couldn't find anywhere to put it. E) The control features didn't work properly.
4 What TWO things does Joe think would improve the computer? A) making it smaller B) reducing the price C) increasing the memory D) increasing the size of the keyboard E) adding more features
why: "The purple and silver make it quite eye-catching" (A) va "thanks to the oval design, it does fit comfortably ... much better" (C). B teskari: "gone too far" (juda kichik). D teskari: ekran qorong'i. E teskari: shovqin "really annoying".

listenings.title: The photography club — evening talk
intro: Foto klub rahbari yangi a'zolarga so'zlamoqda (Section 2 monolog). Avval savollarni o'qing, keyin skriptni bir marta tinglang (ustoz o'qiydi).
transcript: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Photography Club. Let me tell you a bit about what we do.

First, why do people join us? Some come because they've just bought their first proper camera and want to learn how to use it. Others already know the technical side but want to meet people who share the same hobby — that's actually the most common reason. A few hope to sell their photos one day, though I have to say that's quite rare. And some simply want a reason to get out of the house on a cold evening.

Now, our meetings. We meet every Tuesday. On the first Tuesday of the month, we have a guest speaker — usually a professional photographer. On the second, we go out together to take photos, weather permitting. The third Tuesday is for editing on the computer, and on the last one, members show their best work and we discuss it.

What equipment do you need? Well, obviously a camera, though it doesn't have to be expensive — some of our best work is done on phones. You'll also find a tripod useful for evening shots. You don't need editing software of your own, as we have computers here. And please don't bring a printer — we have a professional one at the club.

Finally, the trips. This year we're planning a day at the coast in spring, a weekend in the mountains in summer, and a visit to a city at night to practise with lights. We had hoped to organise a trip abroad, but unfortunately it proved too expensive this year.

listenings.title: Volunteer open day — introduction
intro: Ko'ngillilar tashkiloti muvofiqlashtiruvchisi (Section 2). Avval savollarni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: Hello and thank you all for coming to our volunteer open day. I'll explain how you can help and what we can offer you.

There are several ways to get involved. Some volunteers work in our charity shop, sorting and selling donated items. Others prefer to be outdoors, helping to plant trees and clean up the river. We also need people to answer the phones in the office, and a few volunteers visit elderly people at home. What we no longer do, by the way, is door-to-door collection — we stopped that last year.

Now, what do we ask of you? We ask for at least three hours a week, though many people do more. You don't need any experience, as we provide full training. You do, however, need to be over sixteen, and for the home visits only, you'll need a background check, which we arrange and pay for.

What do you get in return? Well, we can't pay you, of course, but we do cover your travel costs. You also get a free lunch on the days you work, and after six months, we give you a certificate that many people find useful for job applications. Some volunteers say the best thing, though, is simply the friends they make.

listenings.title: Student union — tutorial about a group project
intro: Talaba (Maya) va o'qituvchi (Dr Reed) guruh loyihasi haqida gaplashmoqda (Section 3 suhbat). Uyda bir marta tinglang.
transcript: DR REED: Come in, Maya. So, how's the group project going?
MAYA: Quite well, thanks, though we've had a few problems.
DR REED: Tell me about them.

MAYA: Well, at first we couldn't agree on a topic. Everyone had a different idea. And then, once we chose one, we found it hard to divide the work fairly — some people ended up doing much more than others. The good news is we sorted that out in the end.
DR REED: That's common in group work. Anything else?
MAYA: The biggest issue now is meeting up. We all have different timetables, so finding a time when everyone is free is almost impossible. We tried meeting online, but the connection was often poor.
DR REED: Have you thought about sharing documents online instead of always meeting?
MAYA: Yes, that's worked really well, actually. We use a shared folder, so everyone can add their part whenever they're free. And we keep a list of who's doing what, which stops arguments.
DR REED: Good. Now, for the presentation, what do you still need help with?
MAYA: Two things, really. First, none of us is confident about speaking in front of the class, so any tips would be welcome. And second, we're not sure how much detail to include on the slides.
DR REED: I can help with both. What I wouldn't worry about is the length — twenty minutes is plenty, and you clearly have enough material.

objectives: Summary (xulosa) matnning qaysi qismini qamrab olishini topish: butun matnmi yoki bir-ikki xatboshimi.
Ikki turni farqlash: 1) javob MATNDAN olinadi (so'z chegarasi bilan); 2) javob tayyor RO'YXATDAN (box) tanlanadi.
Bo'sh joy grammatikasidan foydalanish: ot, fe'l, sifat, ko'plik (parosat usuli).
Xulosadagi paraphraseni matndagi asl ibora bilan bog'lash.
Javoblar odatda (USUALLY) matn tartibida kelishini bilib, shundan foydalanish.

intro: Summary completion — matnning qisqa mazmuni beriladi, ichida bo'sh joylar bor. Xulosa matnni boshqa so'zlar bilan qayta aytadi, shuning uchun bu tur 1-darsdagi paraphrase ko'nikmasiga tayanadi.
1-TUR (matndan): "Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage". Javob matndagi so'z bilan, o'zgartirmasdan yoziladi.
2-TUR (box): so'zlar ro'yxati beriladi, ulardan tanlanadi. Ro'yxatdagi so'zlar matnda BOSHQA shaklda bo'lishi mumkin — ma'noga qarang. Ro'yxatda ortiqcha so'zlar bor.
Birinchi qadam: xulosaning sarlavhasi va birinchi gapini o'qing, matnning qaysi qismi ekanini toping. Ba'zan xulosa faqat 1–2 xatboshini qamraydi.
Ikkinchi qadam — parosat: bo'sh joydan oldingi va keyingi so'zga qarab turini aniqlang. "the ___ of" — ot; "to ___ a pen" — fe'l; "a ___ pen" — sifat yoki ot.
Xulosa odatda (USUALLY) matn tartibida boradi: 3-javob 2-javobdan keyin turadi.
Javobni yozgach, butun gapni o'qing: grammatika va ma'no to'g'rimi? "the ___ are identical" — ko'plik ot emas, sifat kerak ekanini ko'rasiz.
presentation: Har doim emas. Sarlavha va birinchi gap qaysi qism ekanini aytadi.
Javobni o'z so'zim bilan yozsam bo'ladimi?
Yo'q. 1-turda matndagi so'z, 2-turda ro'yxatdagi so'z yoziladi.
Box'dagi so'z matnda yo'q, nima qilaman?
Ma'nosini qidiring — box so'zi matndagi so'zning paraphrasei bo'lishi mumkin.
Sifat yoki ot birikmasi: masalan "commercially successful".
Odatda (USUALLY) ha. Topilmasa, kalit so'zga qayting.
Ko'rsatma "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS" bo'lsa, ha.
notes: Summary completion — Passage 2 da ko'p uchraydi. Bu dars 1-dars (paraphrase) va 2-dars (parosat) ko'nikmalarini birlashtiradi.
Har javobdan keyin so'rang: "xulosadagi qaysi so'z matndagi qaysi iboraga teng?"
2-tur (box) uchun ortiqcha so'zlarni o'chirib borish odatini shakllantiring.

Bo'sh joy oldida artikl allaqachon bor

readings.title: Reading #17. Rubik's Cube - How the puzzle achieved success
text: Erno Rubik first studied sculpture and then later architecture in Budapest, where he went on to become a teacher of interior design. It was while he was working as a teacher that he began the preliminary work on an invention that he called the 'Magic Cube'.

Rubik was inspired by geometric puzzles such as the Chinese tangram, a puzzle consisting of various triangles, a square and a parallelogram which can be combined to create different shapes and figures. However, unlike the tangram, which is two-dimensional, Rubik was more interested in investigating how three-dimensional forms, such as the cube, could be moved and combined to produce other forms.

His design consisted of a cube made up of layers of individual smaller cubes, and each smaller cube could be turned in any direction except diagonally. To ensure that the cubes could move independently, without falling apart, Rubik first attempted to join them together using elastic bands. However, this proved to be impossible, so Rubik then solved the problem by assembling them using a rounded interior. This permitted them to move smoothly and easily. He experimented with different ways of marking the smaller cubes, but ended up with the simple solution of giving a different colour to each side. The object was to twist the layers of small cubes so that each side of the large cube was an identical colour.

Rubik took out a patent for the Cube in 1977 and started manufacturing it in the same year. The Cube came to the attention of a Hungarian businessman, Tibor Laczi, who then demonstrated it at the Nuremberg Toy Fair. When British toy expert Tom Kremer saw it, he thought it was amazing and he persuaded a manufacturer, Ideal Toys, to produce 1 million of them in 1979. Ideal Toys renamed the Cube after the toy's inventor, and in 1980, Rubik's Cube was shown at toy fairs all over the world. It won that year's prize in Germany for Best Puzzle. Rubik's Cube is believed to be the world's best-selling puzzle; since its invention, more than 300 million Cubes have been sold worldwide.
paraphrases: can be twisted in almost any way
could be turned in any direction
has sold more than any other

"A cube made up of layers of individual smaller cubes". "Organised in" = "made up of".
"Could be turned in any direction except diagonally". "Though not" = "except". Parosat: "twisted ... though not ___" — ravish kerak.
"Assembling them using a rounded interior. This permitted them to move smoothly". "Allows" = "permitted".
"So that each side of the large cube was an identical colour". "Are ___" — sifat kerak (identity emas).
"Ideal Toys renamed the Cube after the toy's inventor". "Changed the name" = "renamed". "its" dan keyin artikl kerak emas.

The Cube's (4) is shaped in a way that allows the smaller cubes to move smoothly. Each side of the smaller cubes has a different colour, and the aim of the puzzle is to organise the cubes so that the colours on the sides of the large cube are (5). The manufacturers of the puzzle changed the name of the Cube to the name of its (6). It has now sold more than any other (7) in the world.

readings.title: Reading #18. Marcel Bich
text: The man who turned a luxury item into an everyday object

Marcel Bich, a French manufacturer of traditional ink pens, was the man who turned the ballpoint pen into an item that today almost anyone can afford. Bich was appalled at the poor quality of the ballpoint pens that were available, and was also shocked at their high cost. However, he recognised that the ballpoint was a firmly established invention, and he decided to design a cheap pen that worked well and would be commercially successful.

Bich went to the Biro brothers and asked them if he could use the design of their original invention in one of his own pens. In return, he offered to pay them every time he sold a pen. Then, for two years, Bich studied the detailed construction of every ballpoint pen that was being sold, often working with a microscope.

By 1950, he was ready to introduce his new wonder: a plastic pen with a clear barrel that wrote smoothly, did not leak and only cost a few cents. He called it the 'Bic Cristal'. The ballpoint pen had finally become a practical writing instrument. The public liked it immediately, and today it is as common as the pencil. In Britain, they are still called Biros, and many Bic models also say 'Biro' on the side of the pen, to remind people of their original inventors.

Bich became extremely wealthy thanks to his invention, which had worldwide appeal. Over the next 60 years his company, Societe Bic, opened factories all over the world and expanded its range of inexpensive products. Today, Bic is as famous for its lighters and razors as it is for its pens, and you can even buy a Bic mobile phone.

asked them if he could use

readings.title: The sticky note that nobody wanted
text: In 1968 Spencer Silver, a chemist at the American company 3M, was trying to develop a very strong glue for aircraft. Instead, he made the opposite: an adhesive so weak that it could be pulled off a surface without leaving a mark. Silver believed the glue must be useful for something, and for five years he gave talks about it inside the company. Nobody could think of a practical use.

The solution came from a colleague, Art Fry, who sang in a church choir. Every Sunday the paper bookmarks in his hymn book fell out. Fry remembered Silver's glue and put a little on the edge of a bookmark. It stayed in place, and it could be removed without damaging the pages.

The company was not impressed. Managers thought people would never pay for small pieces of paper when free scrap paper was everywhere. A first test in four cities in 1977 failed, because shoppers did not understand what the product was for. The next year, 3M tried a different approach: in the city of Boise, Idaho, it gave free samples to offices. Ninety percent of the people who tried them said they would buy them.

Post-it Notes went on sale across the United States in 1980 and in Europe a year later. Today they are sold in more than 150 countries, and the original yellow colour was chosen by accident — it was the only scrap paper available in the laboratory next door.
paraphrases: nobody could think of a use

readings.title: The invention of the bar code
text: In 1948 a supermarket owner in Philadelphia visited a local university and asked whether there was a way to record product information automatically at the checkout. A graduate student, Bernard Silver, overheard the conversation and told his friend Joseph Woodland, a teacher of mechanical engineering.

Woodland left his job and moved to his grandfather's flat in Florida to think about the problem. Sitting on the beach one day, he pushed his fingers into the sand and pulled them towards him, making four lines. He realised that lines of different widths could be used like the dots and dashes of Morse code. His first design, however, was circular, like a target, so that it could be read from any direction.

The two men received a patent in 1952, but the technology to read the codes did not yet exist. The scanners of the time were enormous and expensive, and the idea was ignored for twenty years. Only when cheap lasers and computers appeared in the early 1970s did supermarkets become interested. A committee chose a rectangular design, which was easier to print than a circle.

The first product ever scanned was a packet of chewing gum, in Ohio, on 26 June 1974. The packet is now kept in a museum in Washington. Today about six billion bar codes are scanned every day, and Woodland, who earned almost nothing from the patent, was given a national medal for technology in 1992.
paraphrases: read without a person writing it

readings.title: The man who made the world wear jeans
text: In 1853 a young German immigrant, Levi Strauss, opened a shop in San Francisco selling cloth, blankets and clothing to the gold miners of California. The miners' trousers wore out quickly, and customers often complained that the pockets tore when they filled them with tools and pieces of gold.

One of Strauss's regular customers was a tailor in Nevada called Jacob Davis. A woman had asked Davis to make strong trousers for her husband, and Davis had the idea of putting small metal pins, called rivets, at the corners of the pockets, the points which usually tore first. The trousers were so successful that other workers soon wanted a pair.

Davis did not have the money to register a patent, which cost 68 dollars, so he wrote to Strauss and offered to share it if Strauss paid. In 1873 the two men received the patent together, and Strauss brought Davis to San Francisco to manage production.

The first "waist overalls", as they were called, were made from a heavy blue cotton cloth called denim. For almost eighty years jeans were working clothes for farmers, miners and factory workers. Only in the 1950s, when film stars wore them on screen, did young people begin to see jeans as fashionable. Today more than two billion pairs are sold every year.
paraphrases: person who often bought from him
be in charge of making the product

Davis could not pay the (4) dollars needed for a patent, so the two men shared it. The first jeans were made of a cloth called (5). intro: Sentence completion — gapning bir qismi beriladi, bo'sh joyni matndagi so'z bilan to'ldirasiz. Javob matndan AYNAN olinadi, o'zgartirilmaydi.
Ko'rsatmani birinchi o'qing: "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS" — bir yoki ikki so'z. Uch so'z yozsangiz, to'g'ri bo'lsa ham 0 ball.
Gaplar matn tartibida keladi (ALWAYS). 3-javob 2-javobdan keyingi joyda turadi.
Parosat: bo'sh joydan oldingi so'zga qarang. "will attack ___" — ot (kimni?); "make it ___" — sifat; "by their ___" — ot; "have a ___ with" — ot.
Gapdagi so'zlar matnda boshqacha aytiladi: "protect themselves" = "if it thinks the human will attack or harm it". Kalit so'zning paraphraseini qidiring.
Tuzoq: matnda javob uch so'zli bo'lishi mumkin ("sense of smell"). Unda gapga mos keladigan va chegaraga sig'adigan qismini yozing ("smell").
Javobni yozgach gapni to'liq o'qing. Grammatika buzilsa (birlik/ko'plik, sifat/ot) — javob noto'g'ri.
presentation: Javobni o'z so'zim bilan yozsam bo'ladimi?
Gapga mos va chegaraga sig'adigan qismini yozing. Masalan "sense of smell" emas, "smell".
Odatda yo'q — artikl gapda allaqachon bor bo'ladi.
Ha, sentence completion javoblari matn tartibida keladi.
Gapning qolgan qismini matn bilan solishtiring — faqat bittasi ma'noga to'liq mos keladi.
notes: Bu dars 2-dars (parosat) va 14-dars (summary completion) ko'nikmalariga tayanadi. Farqi: bu yerda har gap alohida.
Har javobdan keyin so'rang: "gapdagi qaysi so'z matndagi qaysi iboraga teng?"
Ustoz matnining 6-savoli (sense of smell) so'z chegarasi haqida eng yaxshi misol — doskada alohida tahlil qiling.

readings.title: Reading #20. The honey badger
text: It looks harmless and vulnerable. But the honey badger is afraid of nothing... and will attack and eat almost anything

The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is an African and south-Asian mammal that has a reputation for being one of the world's most fearless animals, _despite its small size_. And in spite of its gentle-sounding name, it is also one of its most _aggressive_. Honey badgers have been known to attack lions, buffalo, and snakes three times their size. Even _humans_ are not safe from a honey badger _if it thinks the human will attack or harm it_. They are also extremely tough creatures, and can recover quickly from injuries that would kill most other animals.

At first glance, honey badgers look like the common European badger. They are usually between 75cm and 1 metre long, although males are about twice the size of females. They are instantly _recognisable_ by grey and white stripes that extend from the top of the head to the tail. Closer inspection, which is probably not a wise thing to do, reveals pointed teeth, and sharp front claws which can be four centimetres in length.

Honey badgers are _meat-eating_ animals with an extremely _varied_ diet. They _mainly eat_ a range of _small creatures_ like beetles, lizards and birds, but will also catch larger reptiles like snakes and small crocodiles. Some mammals, such as foxes, antelope and wild cats also form part of their diet.

The badgers _locate their prey_ mainly using their excellent sense of _smell_, and catch most of their prey through digging. During a 24-hour period, they may dig as many as fifty holes, and travel more than 40 kilometres. They are also good climbers, and can easily climb very tall trees to steal eggs from birds' nests, or catch other tree-dwelling creatures.

As their name suggests, honey badgers have always been associated with honey, although they do not actually eat it. It is the highly nutritious bee eggs (called 'brood') that they prefer, and they will do anything to find it. They usually cause a lot of damage to the hive in the process, and for this reason, humans are one of their main predators. Bee-keepers will often set _special traps_ for honey badgers, to protect their hives.

One of the most fascinating aspects of the honey badger is its _working relationship_ with a bird called the greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator). This bird deliberately guides the badger to beehives, then waits while the badger breaks into the hive and extracts the brood. The two creatures, bird and mammal, then share the brood between them.
paraphrases: if it thinks the human will attack or harm it
the pattern and colours on its back
a bird called the greater honeyguide

tasks.title: Questions 1–8: Complete the sentences
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage
tasks.instr: Gaplar matn tartibida (ALWAYS). Javobni gapga qo'yib qayta o'qing.
items: Although they are not big animals, honey badgers are fearless, ___ and tough.
Honey badgers will attack ___ if they need to protect themselves.
The pattern and colours on the honey badger's back make it ___.
The food they eat is meat-based and ___.
___ form the biggest part of a honey badger's diet.
Honey badgers find the creatures they eat by their ___.
___ are often used to catch honey badgers which attack beehives.
For one particular type of food, the honey badger has a ___ with another creature.
why: "One of its most aggressive". "Not big" = "small size". Ikki sifat orasida — sifat kerak.
"Even humans are not safe ... if it thinks the human will attack or harm it". Tuzoq: lions/buffalo — ular himoya uchun emas, umuman hujum qilinadigan hayvonlar.
"Instantly recognisable by grey and white stripes". "Make it + sifat": "recognise" (fe'l) emas.
"Meat-eating animals with an extremely varied diet". "Meat-based" = "meat-eating".
"They mainly eat a range of small creatures". "Mainly eat" = "form the biggest part". Ko'plik ot kerak ("form").
"Locate their prey mainly using their excellent sense of smell". "Sense of smell" — 3 so'z, chegaradan oshadi; "smell" yetarli va gapga mos.
"Bee-keepers will often set special traps for honey badgers". Ko'plik ("are").
"Its working relationship with a bird called the greater honeyguide". Food = brood, another creature = bird.

readings.title: The octopus: a clever escape artist
text: In April 2016, staff at the National Aquarium of New Zealand arrived at work to find that one of their animals had disappeared. Inky, a male octopus, had pushed his way through a small gap at the top of his tank, travelled across the floor, and escaped down a drainpipe that led directly to the sea. The only evidence of his journey was a wet trail on the floor.

Stories like this are not unusual, because octopuses are among the most intelligent animals without a backbone. An octopus has around 500 million nerve cells, a number similar to that of a dog, but about two thirds of them are found not in its head but in its eight arms. As a result, each arm can taste, touch and even make simple decisions on its own.

The octopus is also a master of disguise. Special cells in its skin allow it to change colour in less than a second, so that it can hide against rocks or sand. Some species can even change the texture of their skin to look like coral. When this does not work, an octopus can release a cloud of dark ink, which confuses an attacker and gives the octopus time to swim away.
Its body is unusual in other ways too. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and because it has no bones, it can squeeze through any hole larger than its beak — the only hard part of its body.
Sadly, this remarkable life is short. Most species live for only one or two years, and a female usually dies soon after her eggs hatch, having stopped eating while she guarded them.

tasks.title: Complete the sentences
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage
tasks.instr: Gaplar matn tartibida. Javobni gapga qo'yib o'qing.
items: Inky left his tank through a small ___ at the top.
A ___ on the floor showed where Inky had gone.
Most of an octopus's nerve cells are in its ___.
An octopus can hide by changing its ___ very quickly.
If hiding fails, an octopus may use a cloud of ___ to escape.
The ___ is the only hard part of an octopus's body.
A female octopus stops eating while she is guarding her ___.
why: "Pushed his way through a small gap at the top of his tank".
"The only evidence of his journey was a wet trail on the floor". Evidence = showed.
"About two thirds of them are found ... in its eight arms". "Arms" yoki "eight arms" — ikkalasi ham 2 so'z ichida.
"Change colour in less than a second". Very quickly = less than a second.
"Release a cloud of dark ink".
"Its beak — the only hard part of its body". Artikl gapda bor.
"Having stopped eating while she guarded them" — them = eggs.

tasks.title: So'z chegarasi
why: Gapda "A" allaqachon bor.
"its" gapda bor, 3 so'z bo'lib qoladi.
Matnda "colour" — birlikda.
Javob matndan aynan olinadi.

readings.title: How camels survive the desert
text: Many people believe that a camel stores water in its hump. In fact, the hump is made mostly of fat. When food is scarce, the camel's body breaks down this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and may even fall to one side. A well-fed camel has a firm, upright hump.

The real secret of the camel's survival lies in how it uses water. A camel can lose up to a quarter of its body weight through water loss and still survive, while most mammals would die after losing half that amount. When it finally finds water, it can drink more than 100 litres in about ten minutes.
Its blood is also unusual. The red blood cells of a camel are oval rather than round, which allows them to keep flowing even when the blood becomes thick because the animal is short of water.

Camels also save water by not sweating very much. Their body temperature can rise by around six degrees during a hot day before they begin to sweat, and the heat stored in their body is released during the cold desert night.

Finally, a camel is well protected from sand. It has two rows of long eyelashes, and it can close its nostrils completely during a sandstorm. Wide, soft feet stop it from sinking into the sand, which is why camels are sometimes called "ships of the desert". For thousands of years, these features have made them the most reliable form of transport for people living in dry regions.

tasks.title: Complete the sentences
tasks.type: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage
items: A camel's hump contains mainly ___, not water.
A camel that has eaten well has a firm, ___ hump.
A camel can survive losing about ___ of its weight in water.
After a long time without water, a camel can drink over ___ very quickly.
Because they are ___, a camel's red blood cells can keep moving through thick blood.
Camels lose the heat from their bodies during the ___.
Camels can shut their ___ when there is a sandstorm.
why: "The hump is made mostly of fat". Mainly = mostly.
"A well-fed camel has a firm, upright hump". Eaten well = well-fed.
"Lose up to a quarter of its body weight".
"More than 100 litres in about ten minutes". Over = more than.
"Oval rather than round, which allows them to keep flowing". "Because they are + sifat" — tuzoq: "round" teskari.
"The heat stored in their body is released during the cold desert night". Released = lose.
"It can close its nostrils completely during a sandstorm". Shut = close.

tasks.title: Parosat tekshiruvi
tasks.instr: Bo'sh joy turi va javob mosligini ayting.
why: "contains mainly + ot" — fat.
"about ___ of" — a quarter.
"over ___" — 100 litres.
"they are + sifat" — oval.
"their ___" — nostrils.

readings.title: The return of the wolves
text: By the 1920s, grey wolves had disappeared from Yellowstone, the oldest national park in the United States. Farmers and hunters had killed them to protect their animals, and for the next seventy years the park had no large predator at the top of its food chain.

Without wolves, the number of elk, a large kind of deer, grew quickly. The elk spent long periods feeding beside rivers, where they ate young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Scientists noticed that very few new trees were appearing along the riverbanks.

In 1995 and 1996, thirty-one wolves were caught in Canada and released in the park. Their numbers rose steadily, and within ten years there were more than a hundred. The wolves hunted elk, but they also changed the way elk behaved: the deer began to avoid open river valleys where they could easily be attacked.
In several areas, willow trees started to recover. Beavers, which use willow for food and for building dams, returned in larger numbers, and their dams created pools where fish and birds could live.

However, researchers warn against telling this as a simple story. Hard winters, human hunting and the return of bears also reduced elk numbers, and in some places the trees have not come back at all. Most scientists now agree that the wolves played an important part in the changes, but not the only one — and that nature rarely has a single cause.

tasks.title: Complete the sentences

The wolves brought to the park in the 1990s came from ___.
Elk started to stay away from open ___.
Beavers use willow for food and for building ___.
Researchers say the changes did not have a ___.
why: "Farmers and hunters had killed them".
"The number of elk ... grew quickly".
"Feeding beside rivers". "Riverbanks" ham to'g'ri.
"Thirty-one wolves were caught in Canada".
"Avoid open river valleys". Stay away from = avoid.
"For food and for building dams".
"Nature rarely has a single cause".

intro: Table completion — jadval beriladi, ba'zi kataklar bo'sh. Har ustunning sarlavhasi (name, location, time, type) bo'sh katakka qanday so'z tushishini aytadi.
Jadval odatda qatorma-qator to'ldiriladi: audio birinchi qator (chapdan o'ngga), keyin ikkinchi qator tartibida boradi.
To'ldirilgan kataklar — langar. Masalan, "The World of Ants ... 11 a.m." to'liq bo'lsa, siz ular orasidagi bo'sh kataklarni (location, type) shu voqea haqida gapirilganda tinglaysiz.
Ustun turi so'z turkumini beradi: "location" — joy nomi; "time" — soat; "type of event" — lecture / film / workshop kabi ot.
Paraphrase: jadvalda "location", audioda "in the Insect House" yoki "held in Room 27".
Tuzatish tuzog'i: "the lecture room, no, sorry, correct that — the main hall". Oxirgi javob yoziladi.
presentation: Qatorma-qator, chapdan o'ngga. Audio jadval tartibida boradi.
To'liq kataklarga qarang — ular sizni keyingi bo'sh katakka olib boradi.
So'z turini aytadi: location → joy, time → soat, type → tadbir turi.
Yo'q, lekin nomlar (Insect House, Theatre C) katta harf bilan tabiiy ko'rinadi.
notes: Ikkala ustoz audiosi ham hayvonlar/tabiat mavzusida tadbirlar jadvali — bir xil format, o'quvchi ikkinchisida mustaqil ishlaydi.
Ustoz kaliti yuborilgan va javoblarga kiritildi (Track 27 va Track 12).
Har javobdan keyin so'rang: "jadvaldagi qaysi ustun edi? audioda qaysi so'z bilan aytildi?"
Tuzatish tuzoqlari (main hall, correct that) doskada alohida ko'rsatiladi.

listenings.title: Track 27. Animal World — today's events
intro: Animal World markazidagi bugungi tadbirlar e'loni. Avval jadvalni o'rganing: har ustun (location, type of event, time) qanday so'z kerakligini aytadi. To'liq kataklar (11 a.m., film, demonstration) — langar. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS OR A NUMBER for each answer.
transcript: Hi there, everybody, and welcome to Animal World. Before you start your visit, I'd just like to tell you about a few special events happening here today. They're all free, and I'd really encourage you to go to as many of them as you can, as I think you'll learn a lot.

The first event is called The World of Ants, and it's happening this morning quite soon, in the Insect House, which is just a short walk from here. The well-known entomologist Dr David Crocker, who many of you will have seen on television, is giving a lecture all about ants – the different types of ants, how they organise themselves, what they eat, their behaviour and so on. It's actually a fascinating subject. So, The World of Ants, a lecture by Dr Crocker, in the Insect House, and it starts at 11 o'clock and lasts for 60 minutes.

At midday, that's 12 o'clock, there's a film which is just as fascinating and it's called The Great Migration. This is all about birds and how they migrate across continents and oceans using the Sun, the stars and the Earth's magnetic field. As I said, it's a film – an absolutely spectacular film – which all the family will enjoy, some fabulous photography, and it's on in Theatre C, which you can see just behind me – so bear that in mind for 12 o'clock.

The next event is a demonstration taking place in the Exhibition Room and given by Monica Chaddha. It's called Encouraging Garden Wildlife. Monica will be showing you ways of encouraging animals, birds and other wildlife to visit and live in your garden, how to place boxes for nests, what food to put out for them and all sorts of practical advice. That's at 2.30, so just after lunch.

The final free event for today is Birds of Prey. Tasha, their keeper, will be giving a display of some of our most magnificent birds and how they fly, and I thoroughly recommend this event. The display includes eagles, vultures and owls and will be starting at 3.45 on the lawn outside. It's an unforgettable experience, so remember, on the front lawn at 3.45 to see the birds flying.

listenings.title: Track 12. College Natural History day — morning events
intro: Kollej direktori talabalarga ertalabki tadbirlar haqida aytmoqda. Har talaba bittasini tanlashi kerak. Avval jadvalni o'qing, keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS OR A NUMBER for each answer.
transcript: Hello, everyone, and welcome to our college Natural History day. You've all got your programme for the day, but let me just give you a bit of information about your options for this morning's sessions, which begin at half past nine. Remember, you need to attend one of these three sessions.

All right, your first choice is called 'Dogs might fly', which will take place in Room 27. Professor Keenan, who you may remember ran a workshop last year on how dinosaurs became extinct, will be giving a lecture on the evolution of animals. In particular, she'll be looking at how they may evolve in the future, and this will be followed by a group discussion where you'll get a chance to ask her questions and offer your own thoughts and opinions on this. So, if the evolution of animals is something you're interested in, head for Room 27.

We all know that animals communicate with each other, but what about flowers? Your second choice is a video presentation called 'Flowers talk'. This considers the possibility that plants and flowers do actually communicate with each other. The video is presented by Patrick Bell, who has just written a book on how plants adapt to their natural environment, so it should be very interesting. That will take place in the lecture room, no, sorry, correct that, here in the main hall. We've had to move it because the lecture room is being renovated.

The third choice is ideal for those of you who want to get a bit of fresh air. We've called it 'A world in your garden', which we thought was appropriate as it looks at the sort of things you can find just by stepping out of your front door. Anyway, for those of you interested in getting away from the classroom, Doctor Watkins will be taking you on a nature walk through the local park, and she'll be telling you about some of the fascinating animals and plants that live and grow nearby. And it's a lovely day for a walk!

The final option, well, you might want to avoid this one if you're frightened of things like snakes, as this is a hands-on workshop where you'll actually get a chance to handle these exotic creatures. It won't just be snakes, however. I believe Tom Howard, our resident reptile expert, has brought some other reptiles along for you to meet, including his pet tortoise, Reggie, who is over 100 years old, and a pet lizard he calls Arthur. So, if you want to meet Reggie and his other reptile friends, head on over to the Biology lab at 9.30.

intro: Jamoa markazi xodimi haftalik darslar jadvalini aytmoqda. Avval jadvalni o'qing, keyin bir marta tinglang.
transcript: Welcome to the Greenfield Community Centre. Let me run through our weekly classes so you can decide which suit you.
On Monday evenings we have a cookery class. It's held in the kitchen, of course, and it costs eight pounds a session. It's very popular, so please book ahead.
On Wednesdays there's a painting class in the art room. It runs from six to eight, and you should bring your own brushes, although we provide the paint.
Thursday is our busiest day. In the afternoon there's a yoga class in the main hall, which is free for members. And in the evening, the same hall is used for a dance class, which costs five pounds.

Finally, on Saturday mornings we run a photography class. This one meets in the computer room rather than a studio, because most of the work is editing pictures. It's suitable for beginners, and the teacher is a professional photographer.

Tinglashdan oldin xaritada "You are here" nuqtasini, yo'llarni va belgilangan joylarni topish.
So'zlovchi bilan birga xarita bo'ylab "yurish" — har yo'nalishdan keyin qayerda ekanini kuzatish.

intro: Map labelling — xarita yoki bino rejasi beriladi, joylar harflar (A–G) bilan belgilangan. Siz har nom (gift shop, café) qaysi harfga to'g'ri kelishini yozasiz.
BIRINCHI qadam: "You are here" yoki "entrance" ni toping. So'zlovchi har doim shu nuqtadan boshlaydi.
So'zlovchi xarita bo'ylab tartib bilan "yuradi". Savollar ham odatda (USUALLY) shu tartibda keladi. Qalam bilan yo'lni kuzating.
ENG MUHIM: "on your left / on your right" — yurayotgan odamning chap-o'ngi. Agar u xaritada pastga qarab yursa, uning o'ngi sizning chapingiz bo'ladi. Xaritani aylantirib qarash ham mumkin.
Yo'nalish so'zlari: turn left / turn right, go straight ahead, go past, cross, take the first right, at the crossroads / junction / roundabout.
Joylashuv so'zlari: opposite (qarshisida), next to (yonida), between (orasida), at the corner of (burchagida), just beyond / just over (sal narida), at the end of (oxirida).
Tuzoq: bir necha joy tilga olinadi, lekin faqat savoldagisi javob. "Don't go too far, or you'll come to the aquarium" — akvarium savolda yo'q, u faqat chegara.
presentation: Yo'q! Yurayotgan odamning chapi. Pastga yursa — teskari bo'ladi.
Keyingi langarni kuting (lake, reception, crossroad) va o'sha joydan davom eting.
Odatda yo'q. Ba'zi harflar umuman ishlatilmaydi.
notes: Darsni yo'nalish so'zlari bilan boshlang: doskada strelkalar chizib, turn left / right, go past, cross, opposite, next to, between, at the corner of, T-junction, Y-junction, crossroads, roundabout, traffic lights, zebra crossing so'zlarini ko'rsating.
Track 28 (hayvonot bog'i) — oson: bitta yo'l, aniq langarlar (lake, penguins). Track 13 (kollej rejasi) — eng qiyin: ko'p xona, eshiklar va koridorlar. Shuning uchun u darsning OXIRIDA.
Track 28 uchun ustoz kaliti yuborilmagan — javoblar skript bo'yicha yechildi. Track 13 kaliti ustozniki (1 D, 2 E, 3 K, 4 C, 5 B).
Xaritalar asl kitob rasmidagi joylashuv bo'yicha Jony Academy tomonidan qayta chizilgan.
mistakes: Tilga olingan har joyni javob deb o'ylash

listenings.title: Track 28. Zoo — directions from the main building
intro: Hayvonot bog'ida xodim tashrif buyuruvchilarga yo'l ko'rsatmoqda. Avval xaritada "You are here" va "main building" ni toping. Yo'l qayerda ikkiga ayriladi? Lake va penguins qayerda? Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write the correct letter, A–G, next to questions 1–3.
transcript: Now, I'll just give you a few directions before you leave, especially for those of you who are feeling a bit hungry. When you leave the main building, you come to an area where the path divides. If you take the right-hand path, you'll see the lake on your right, and exactly opposite the lake on your left is the gift shop. Apart from selling gifts, it sells snacks, sandwiches and light drinks. If you walk on past the lake, on your right you'll also see the penguins. Go past the penguins and you'll come to the restaurant, also on your right. Don't go too far, or you'll come to the aquarium. The aquarium is on your right at the crossroad, and just over the crossroad, also on your right, is the lion enclosure.

If you're thinking of having a picnic, the best place to go is the picnic area, and for this you need to turn left at the crossroad and walk along a few metres. At the end of the path, you'll find the picnic area on your left.
Now, if you have any questions, I'd be happy to answer them and, once again, I really hope you enjoy your visit. Thank you.

tasks.title: Questions 1–3: Write the correct letter, A–G
tasks.instr: So'zlovchi bilan xarita bo'ylab yuring. Chap/o'ng — yuruvchiniki.
why: "The path divides ... take the right-hand path ... the lake on your right, and exactly opposite the lake on your left is the gift shop". O'ng yo'lda yuqoriga yursangiz, ko'l o'ngda, uning qarshisida chapda — F.

"Walk on past the lake ... on your right ... the penguins. Go past the penguins and you'll come to the restaurant, also on your right". Penguinsdan keyingi o'ngdagi joy — E. Tuzoq: D — akvarium ("on your right at the crossroad"), C — sher qo'rasi ("just over the crossroad").

"Turn left at the crossroad and walk along a few metres. At the end of the path ... on your left". Chapga burilgach (g'arbga), chap tomon — janub; yo'l oxirida — A. Tuzoq: B — yo'l boshida, oxirida emas.

intro: Park xodimi darvoza oldida tashrif buyuruvchilarga yo'l ko'rsatmoqda. Avval "main gate" ni toping. Skriptni ustoz bir marta o'qiydi.
transcript: Welcome to Riverside Park. You're standing at the main gate, so let me tell you where everything is.
As soon as you come in, you'll see the café straight away on your right. It's a good place for a hot drink on a cold day. The toilets are just opposite, on your left.

If you walk straight up the main path, just before you reach the crossroads, you'll see the pond on your right. That's where you can hire a boat — the boat hire hut is right next to the pond, on your right.
For those of you with children, the playground is a little further. When you get to the crossroads, turn left, and at the end of that path, on your right, you'll find the playground.

The first shop on your left is a sports shop, and the second shop on your left is the bookshop, which has a small café inside.

listenings.title: Track 13. College plan — for visiting students
listenings.qtype: Plan labelling (1–5) — eng qiyin, oxirgi mashq
intro: Kollejga kelgan talabalarga bino rejasi tushuntirilmoqda. Bu eng qiyin mashq: ko'p xona, koridorlar va eshiklar. Avval rejada "College entrance", "Reception", "Sports Hall" va "Parking area for bicycles" ni toping. Keyin BIR MARTA tinglang.
Ko'rsatma: Write the correct letter, A–K, next to questions 1–5.
transcript: OK, now, we've got some students here from Bardwell College who have joined us for today's events. Hello to you all, and welcome.

Now, before our day begins, you'll need to get a guest badge, which you'll have to wear while you're on the college premises. You can get these from the administration office. To get there from the main hall, leave the hall by the door opposite reception, turn left, and just follow the corridor to the end. The administration office is on your right. Don't go any further, or you'll be in the sports hall. If you show your guest badge in the café, by the way, you'll get a 20% discount on drinks and sandwiches.

To get there from the main hall, walk along the corridor between the main hall and reception and turn right. The café is through the first door on your left. Directly opposite the café, on the same corridor, is the student common room, where you can go to relax and perhaps meet some of our own students.

If you have any valuables that you don't want to carry around with you, I suggest you put these in a locker. These are next to the sports hall, opposite the administration office. You can get a key for a locker when you get your guest badge from the administration office.

And if you want to use our library, leave the main hall by the door opposite the one you came in – that's the door by the bicycle parking area – and walk to the end of the corridor. The library is through the door straight ahead of you.

"Walk along the corridor between the main hall and reception and turn right. The café is through the first door on your left". O'ngga burilgach, chap tomondagi birinchi eshik — E.
"Directly opposite the café, on the same corridor". E ning qarshisi — K.
"Next to the sports hall, opposite the administration office". D ning qarshisi, sport zali yonida — C.
"Leave the main hall by the door ... by the bicycle parking area – and walk to the end of the corridor. The library is through the door straight ahead of you". Koridor oxirida to'g'ri oldinda — B.

lessons.title: Reading: Pick from a List (Choose TWO)
lessons.grammar_topic: Pick from a list — ro'yxatdan ikki (yoki uch) javob tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Jony Academy materiali — ustoz matnlari (#21, #22) va mualliflik matnlari.
objectives: "Choose TWO letters" savolida ikkala javobni ham matndan isbotlash.
Savol qaysi mavzuni so'rayotganini aniqlab, matnning tegishli qismini tez topish.
Har bir variantni alohida tekshirish: matnda bormi? savolga javobmi? aynan shundaymi?
Tuzoqlarni ajratish: matnda bor, lekin boshqa narsa haqida; qisman to'g'ri; teskari.
5 ta matnda ishlash: ustozning 2 matni + 3 ta Jony Academy matni.
timeline: Salomlashish, o'tgan darsdagi savol turini 3 savolda eslatish
Ustoz doskada: qoida, bosqichlar, tipik xatolar
Savol turiga oid mashq birga bajariladi, har javob izohlanadi
Matndagi va savoldagi so'zlar jadvali; o'quvchilar ovoz chiqarib topadi
Mustaqil bajariladi, keyin javoblar izoh bilan tekshiriladi
Skript ustoz tomonidan o'qiladi yoki audio qo'yiladi, keyin transkript bilan tekshiriladi
Xatolar daftari: har xato javob sababi bilan yoziladi

intro: Pick from a list — savol va 5 ta variant (A–E) beriladi. Ulardan IKKITASI to'g'ri (ba'zan uchtasi). Ko'rsatmada "Choose TWO letters" yoziladi.
Ikkala javob ham alohida ball oladi: 1–2-savol = 2 ball. Birini topsangiz ham 1 ball olasiz, shuning uchun bo'sh qoldirmang.
Javoblarni istalgan tartibda yozish mumkin: "B, C" yoki "C, B" — ikkalasi ham to'g'ri.
Bu savollar ko'pincha matnning BIR xatboshisiga tegishli. Savoldagi kalit so'zni (whale near Brazil, male badgers) matndan toping va o'sha qismni diqqat bilan o'qing.
Har variant uchun uchta savol: 1) matnda bormi? 2) savolda so'ralgan narsa haqidami? 3) aynan shundaymi yoki kuchliroq/teskari?
Asosiy tuzoq: variant matnda bor, lekin boshqa odam, boshqa vaqt yoki boshqa guruh haqida. Masalan: "female badgers never socialised WITH EACH OTHER" — bu "erkaklar bilan aralashmaydi" degani emas.
Variantlar matnda boshqa so'zlar bilan aytiladi: "took a picture" = "photographed"; "lost her way" = "did not know where she was going".
presentation: Uni yozing va ikkinchisiga eng ehtimollisini tanlang — har biri alohida ball.
Yo'q. "B, C" va "C, B" bir xil.
Uchinchisini qayta tekshiring: u savolga javobmi yoki matnda boshqa narsa haqida aytilganmi?
Odatda ha, lekin bitta savol bir nechta xatboshini qamrashi mumkin.
Javob varag'ida ikki qator — har biriga bitta harf.
notes: Ustoz har variant uchun "bor / savolga emas / teskari / aytilmagan" belgisini qo'ydiradi — bu darsning asosiy ishi.
Humpback whale matnidagi 9–10-savolni doskada tahlil qiling: matn janub haqida gapiradi ("hostile", "hard to get to"), javob esa shimol haqida — teskari fikrlash kerak.
Honey badger matnida 3-savol E varianti eng yaxshi tuzoq misoli.
mistakes: So'z bor, lekin boshqa narsa haqida
Teskari fikrlashni unutish (janub qiyin → shimol oson)

class_ex.title: Bormi? Savolga javobmi?
class_ex.instr: Ustoz matndan bir gap va bir variant o'qiydi; o'quvchi "to'g'ri / boshqa narsa haqida / teskari / aytilmagan" deydi.
items: Gap: "Female badgers never socialised with each other." Variant: Female badgers do not mix with male badgers.
Gap: "They're actually quite sociable creatures around humans." Variant: They do not enjoy human company.
Gap: "Photographed its tail fluke." Variant: They took a picture.
Gap: "Photographed its tail fluke." Variant: They marked its tail.
Gap: "Fortunately this is rare, but it does happen." Variant: It is common for them to attack people.
why: Matn urg'ochilar O'ZARO aralashmasligini aytadi, erkaklar haqida emas.
Sociable = ular odamlar bilan yaxshi.
Photographed = took a picture.
Dumi suratga olingan, belgilanmagan.
Rare ≠ common.
class_ex.note: To'rt javob turi doskada yozib qo'yiladi va butun dars davomida ishlatiladi.

readings.title: Reading #21. Humpback whale breaks migration record
text: A whale surprises researchers with her journey.
A lone humpback whale travelled more than 9,800 kilometres from breeding areas in Brazil to those in Madagascar, setting a record for the longest mammal migration ever documented.

Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) are known to have some of the longest migration distances of all mammals, and this huge journey is about 400 kilometres _farther_ than the previous humpback record. The finding was made by Peter Stevick, a biologist at the College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor, Maine.

The whale's journey was unusual not only for its _length_, but also because it travelled across almost 90 degrees of longitude _from west to east_. Typically, humpbacks move in a north-south direction between _cold feeding areas_ and _warm breeding grounds_ - and the longest journeys which have been recorded until now have been between breeding and feeding sites.

The whale, a female, was first spotted off the coast of Brazil, where researchers _photographed_ its tail fluke and _took skin samples_ for chromosome testing to determine the animal's sex. Two years later, a tourist on a whale-watching boat snapped a photo of the humpback near Madagascar.

To match the two sightings, Stevick's team used an extensive international catalogue of photographs of the undersides of tail flukes, which have distinctive markings. Researchers routinely _compare the markings_ in each new photograph to those in the archive.

The scientists then estimated the animal's shortest possible route: an arc _skirting the southern tip of South Africa_ and heading north-east towards Madagascar. The minimum distance is 9,800 kilometres, says Stevick, but this is likely to be an underestimate, because the whale probably took a detour to feed on krill in the Southern Ocean _near Antarctica_ before reaching its destination.

Most humpback-whale researchers focus their efforts on the Northern Hemisphere because the Southern Ocean near the Antarctic is _a hostile environment_ and it is _hard to get to_, explains Rochelle Constantine, who studies the ecology of humpback whales at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. But, for whales, oceans in the Southern Hemisphere are wider and easier to travel across, says Constantine. Scientists will probably observe more long-distance migrations in the Southern Hemisphere as _satellite tracking_ becomes increasingly common, she adds.

Daniel Palacios, an oceanographer at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, says that the record-breaking journey could indicate that migration patterns are shifting as populations begin to recover from near-extinction and the population increases. But the reasons why the whale did not follow the usual migration routes remain a mystery. She could have been _exploring new habitats_, or simply have _lost her way_. 'We generally think of humpback whales as very well studied, but then they surprise us with things like this,' Palacios says. 'Undoubtedly there are a lot of things we still don't know about whale migration.'

readings.title: Reading #22. On the trail of the honey badger
readings.qtype: Pick from a list (1–5) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: Researchers learn more about this fearless African predator

On a recent field trip to the Kalahari Desert, a team of researchers learnt a lot more about honey badgers. They were rewarded with a detailed insight into how these fascinating creatures live and hunt.

The team employed a local wildlife expert, Kitso Khama, to help them locate and follow the badgers across the desert. Their main aim was _to study the badgers' movements and behaviour_ as discreetly as possible, without frightening them away or causing them to change their natural behaviour. They also planned _to trap a few and study them close up before releasing them_. In view of the animal's reputation, this was something that even Khama was reluctant to do.

'The problem with honey badgers is they are naturally _curious_ animals, especially when they see _something new_,' he says. 'That, combined with their _unpredictable_ nature, can be a dangerous mixture. If they sense you have food, for example, they won't be shy about coming right up to you for something to eat. They're actually quite sociable creatures around humans, but as soon as they feel they might be in danger, they can become extremely vicious. Fortunately this is _rare_, but it does happen.'

The research confirmed many things that were already known. As expected, honey badgers ate any creatures they could catch and kill. Even poisonous snakes, feared and avoided by most other animals, were not safe from them. The researchers were surprised, however, by the animal's fondness for local _melons_, probably because of their _high water content_. Previously researchers thought that the animal got all of its liquid requirements from its prey. The team also learnt that, contrary to previous research findings, the badgers occasionally formed _loose family groups_. They were also able to confirm certain results from previous research, including the fact that female badgers never socialised _with each other_.

Following some of the male badgers was a challenge, since they can cover large distances in a short space of time. Some hunting territories cover _more than 500 square kilometres_. Although they seem happy to share these territories with other males, there are _occasional fights_ over an important food source, and male badgers can be as aggressive towards each other as they are towards other species.

As the badgers became accustomed to the presence of people, it gave the team the chance to get up close to them _without being the subject of the animals' curiosity_ - or their sudden aggression. The badgers' eating patterns, which had been disrupted, returned to normal. It also allowed the team to observe more closely some of the other creatures that form working associations with the honey badger, as these seemed to _adopt the badgers' relaxed attitude_ when near humans.

readings.title: Why birds fly in a V
text: Anyone who has watched geese crossing an autumn sky has noticed their V-shaped formation. For a long time, scientists suspected that the shape helped birds save energy, but it was very difficult to prove, because it is hard to measure what a bird is doing in the air.

In 2014, a team from the Royal Veterinary College in London found a solution. They attached tiny data recorders to a group of northern bald ibises, rare birds that had been trained to follow a light aircraft on their migration. The recorders measured the position of each bird and every beat of its wings.

The results were surprising. Each bird flew in exactly the place where the air pushed up by the wings of the bird in front could help lift it. The birds also timed their wing beats to match the bird ahead, so that they always met rising air rather than falling air. Earlier research on pelicans had shown that birds flying in formation have lower heart rates than those flying alone.

Flying at the front is the hardest job, and no single bird does it all the time. The ibises regularly changed places, and each bird spent roughly as long leading as it did following — a kind of fair sharing that researchers had not expected.

Energy is not the only reason for the shape. A V also allows every bird to see the others clearly, which helps the group stay together and avoid collisions. Young birds on their first migration can follow experienced adults who know the route.

readings.title: The dance of the honeybee
text: When a honeybee discovers a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a dance. For centuries, beekeepers noticed this strange movement, but it was the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch who first explained what it meant. His work on bee communication won him a share of the Nobel Prize in 1973.

Von Frisch found that bees use two main dances. If the flowers are close to the hive, a bee performs a "round dance", running in small circles. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not the exact direction. For food further away, the bee performs a "waggle dance": it runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement.

The waggle dance contains surprisingly precise information. The angle of the straight run compared with a vertical line on the honeycomb shows the direction of the food compared with the position of the sun. The length of time the bee spends waggling shows how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the greater the distance.

The dancer also shares other clues. Other bees touch it with their antennae and learn the smell of the flowers it has visited, and they may taste samples of nectar it brings back. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, bees also adjust the angle of their dance as time passes.
Not every scientist accepted von Frisch's ideas at first. Some believed that bees found food only by smell, and it took several decades of experiments before the dance language was widely accepted.

readings.title: How animals sleep
text: All animals with a brain seem to need some form of sleep, but the way they sleep varies enormously. Some of the most unusual examples come from animals that cannot simply lie down and close their eyes.

Dolphins, for example, must come to the surface to breathe, so they can never become fully unconscious. Instead, they rest one half of the brain at a time, while the other half stays awake to control breathing and watch for danger. During this kind of sleep, a dolphin often keeps one eye open.

Frigatebirds, which fly over the ocean for weeks without landing, use a similar method. In 2016, scientists fitted small devices to their heads and discovered that the birds slept in the air, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both. However, they slept for only about forty minutes a day in flight, compared with more than twelve hours on land.
At the other extreme, some bats sleep for up to twenty hours a day. Scientists believe this saves energy and keeps them away from danger at times when the insects they eat are not active.

Large grazing animals sleep much less. Giraffes and elephants in the wild may sleep for only two to four hours, often in short periods, because they need to spend a long time eating and must stay alert to predators. Why sleep is so necessary is still not fully understood, but its loss causes serious problems in every animal that has been studied.

intro: Yes / No / Not Given — 6-darsdagi True / False / Not Given ning "fikr" varianti. Savol faktni emas, MUALLIF NIMA DEB O'YLASHINI so'raydi.
YES — gap muallif fikriga mos. NO — gap muallif fikriga qarshi. NOT GIVEN — muallif bu haqda fikr bildirmagan (balki umuman gapirmagan).
Muallif fikri odatda baho so'zlari bilan beriladi: kindness, unusual, better off, the truth is, not good news, should. Shu so'zlarni belgilang.
Tuzoq 1 — gapda baho bor, matnda yo'q: "Into the Wild is a GOOD title" — muallif nom haqida baho bermagan → NOT GIVEN.
Tuzoq 2 — miqdor: "MANY young people make the same decisions" — matn "most would not do the same thing" deydi → NO.
Tuzoq 3 — taqqoslash: "more adventurous THAN OTHERS" — matn "more conventional than others" deydi → NO.
Savollar matn tartibida keladi (ALWAYS). NOT GIVEN javobi ham ikki qo'shni javob orasidagi joyda qidiriladi.

readings.title: Reading #23. Making a change
text: How easy is it for us to change our lives – and why?

In 1990, a young American named Christopher McCandless gave up his career plans, left behind everyone he knew, including his family, and went off on an adventure. He was 22 at the time. _In an act of kindness_, he donated all his savings to the famous charity, Oxfam International, and hitchhiked his way through America to Alaska. His decisions were so unusual for his age that Jon Krakauer wrote a book about them called Into the Wild, and Sean Penn directed a film that had the same title.

Of course, this is an unusual story. _Most college graduates would not do quite the same thing._ However, studies do show that _in teenage years, people are more likely to try out new experiences_. Instead of following the family career path, for example, and working his way up the same organization like his grandfather did, a 15-year-old may dream about becoming a traveller - only to find _in his early 20s that this fascination with new places is declining_ and change is less attractive. This age-related trend can be observed in all cultures.

The reason why people all over the world become less keen to change as they get older may be because people's lives generally _follow similar patterns and involve similar demands_. Most people, _wherever they are_, aim to find a job and a partner. As they get older, they may have young children to look after and possibly elderly family members. These responsibilities cannot be achieved without some degree of consistency, which means that new experiences and ideas may not have a place in the person's life. New experiences may bring excitement but also insecurity, and so most people prefer to stay with the familiar.

However, not every individual is the same. One toddler may want to play a different game every day and _get fed up if nothing changes_ at the nursery. Another may seek out and play with the same children and toys on every visit. _Young children who avoid new experiences will grow up to be more conventional than others._ Psychologists argue that those who have more open personalities as children are more open than others might be when they are older. They also suggest that young men have a greater interest in novelty than women, although, as they age, this desire for new experiences fades more quickly than it does in women.

The truth is that, as we get older, we prefer the things we know. We tend to order the same meals in restaurants, sit on the same side of the train when we commute to work, go on holiday to the same places and construct our day in the same way. If you are older than 20, remember that your openness to new experiences is slowly declining. So _you are better off making a new start today than postponing it until later_.
paraphrases: many young people make the same decisions
most college graduates would not do the same thing
more ready to have new experiences
more likely to try out new experiences
wherever they are / in all cultures
get fed up if nothing changes

readings.title: Reading #24. Breaking the habit
readings.qtype: Yes / No / Not Given (1–7) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: We all think we can break our bad habits — but they can stay with us for life

What is a bad habit? The most common definition is that it is something that we do regularly, almost without thinking about it, and which has some sort of negative consequence. This consequence could affect those around us, or it could affect us personally. Those who deny having bad habits are probably lying. Bad habits are part of what makes us human.

Many early habits, like sucking our thumb, are _broken when we are very young_. We are either _told to stop doing it by our parents, or_ we consciously or subconsciously _observe that others do not have the same habit_, and we gradually grow out of it. It is when we intentionally or unintentionally _pick up new habits in our later childhood or early adulthood_ that it becomes a problem. Unless we can break that habit early on, it becomes a part of our life, and becomes 'programmed' into our brain.

A recent study of human memory suggests that no matter how hard we try to change our habits, it is the old ways that tend to win, especially in situations where we are _rushed, stressed or overworked_. Habits that we thought we had got rid of can _suddenly come back_. During the study programme, the researchers showed a group of volunteers several pictures, and gave them words to associate with them (for example, see a picture of tea, and associate it with 'breakfast'). They then showed the volunteers the same pictures again, and gave them new words to associate with them (see a picture of tea, and say 'afternoon').

A few days later, the volunteers were given a test. The researchers showed them the pictures, and told them to respond with one of the words they had been given for each one. _It came as no surprise_ that their answers were split between the first set of words and the second. Two weeks later, they were given the same test again. This time, most of them only gave the first set of words. They appeared to have completely forgotten the second set. The study confirms that _the responses we learn first are those that remain strongest over time_. We may try to change our ways, but after a while, the response that comes to mind first is usually the first one we learned. The more that response is used, the more automatic it becomes and the harder it becomes to respond in any other way.

The study therefore suggests that over time, our bad habits also become automatic, learned behaviour. This is _not good news for people who picked up bad habits early in life and now want to change or break them_. Even when we try to put new, good intentions into practice, those previously learned habits remain stronger in more automatic, unconscious forms of memory.
paraphrases: (early habits) broken when we are very young
told by parents OR observe others
(opposite of) it came as no surprise
not good news ... want to change or break them
